prompt: What is Playwright?
options: A framework for automating browsers and testing web apps
A framework for testing isolated JavaScript functions and mocks
A framework for bundling browser assets before release
A framework for linting accessibility rules in source
explanation: Playwright drives real browsers to test apps end to end.

prompt: Which browsers can Playwright control?
options: Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browser engines
Chromium and Firefox, but not the WebKit engine
Chromium and WebKit, but not the Firefox engine
Only the browser installed as the system default
explanation: Playwright supports all three major engines.

prompt: What is an end-to-end (E2E) test?
options: A test of a user journey through the running application
A test of one component with its backend services replaced
A test of an API handler without a browser session
A test of data types before the application starts
explanation: E2E tests validate full user flows across the real stack.

prompt: What does page.goto() do?
options: Navigates the page to the supplied URL
Sends a request without changing the page
Opens the supplied URL in a second tab
Changes only the address shown in the bar
explanation: goto loads the given URL in the page.

prompt: What does a locator represent?
options: A query that finds matching elements when used
A cached reference to one fixed DOM element from an earlier query
A matcher for outgoing network requests
A selector for choosing a browser project
explanation: Locators describe how to find and act on elements.

prompt: What do Playwright's auto-waits do?
options: Wait for actionability conditions before an action
Pause for a fixed delay before every action regardless of page state
Retry the entire test after each failed action
Wait only for all network requests to finish
explanation: Actions wait until elements are visible/enabled, reducing flakiness.

prompt: What is a recommended locator strategy?
options: Prefer roles and accessible names that users perceive
Prefer positional CSS selectors tied to the current page layout
Prefer generated class names from the style build
Prefer XPath paths rooted at the document body
explanation: Resilient, user-facing locators survive markup changes.

prompt: What does the trace viewer provide?
options: A timeline of actions and captured test state
A dashboard of coverage across all source files
A baseline image for comparing visual changes
A summary of only the final assertion failures
explanation: Traces capture snapshots, actions, and network for post-mortem debugging.

prompt: How does Playwright isolate tests?
options: A separate browser context for each test by default
One shared context with a new tab for each test
One shared context whose cookies are reused by tests
A new browser installation before every test
explanation: Each test gets an isolated context (cookies/storage), like a clean incognito session.

prompt: What is a fixture in Playwright?
options: Reusable setup and resources supplied to tests
A static file containing expected page markup for each assertion
A browser extension loaded before each test
A screenshot saved at the end of each test
explanation: Fixtures supply prepared objects (page, auth, data) to tests.

prompt: Why do auto-waits reduce flakiness?
options: They wait for an actionable target when actions run
They repeat each failed step after a fixed pause, even when ready
They make the browser execute every action twice
They delay all tests until the whole page is idle
explanation: Waiting on actionability avoids race conditions from hardcoded delays.

prompt: What is the benefit of browser contexts?
options: Isolated sessions within one browser process
A shared session with faster tab switching
A separate operating system process per page
Real mobile hardware for every test run
explanation: Contexts are cheap, isolated profiles within one browser process.

prompt: What does a web-first assertion (expect) do?
options: It retries a supported condition until success or timeout
It runs a single immediate check without retrying as the UI updates
It retries the entire test after a mismatch occurs
It changes the page state until the check passes
explanation: Playwright's expect polls the condition, smoothing over async UI updates.

prompt: Why prefer getByRole over CSS selectors?
options: It targets accessible meaning rather than DOM structure
It ignores the accessible name and matches the element's CSS path
It matches any element with the same CSS class
It disables Playwright's actionability checks
explanation: Role-based queries reflect how users/AT perceive the UI and resist refactors.

prompt: How does Playwright run tests in parallel?
options: Worker processes execute tests concurrently
Assertions inside one test execute concurrently
Each individual action starts its own worker
Every test runs sequentially on one worker
explanation: Workers execute different spec files at once for speed.

prompt: What is the root cause of E2E flakiness, and Playwright's mitigation?
options: Race conditions; use actionability waits and retrying assertions
Browser crashes; restart the browser after every failed interaction
Selector syntax; replace every locator with XPath
Network latency; insert the same sleep after each step
explanation: Most flakiness is timing-related; auto-waits and web-first assertions address it.

prompt: How does sharding speed up large E2E suites?
options: It divides test work among parallel CI jobs
It makes each test skip its slowest assertions
It replays one test concurrently in many tabs
It removes test files after their first pass
explanation: Sharding distributes the suite so total wall-clock time drops.

prompt: What does network interception/mocking enable?
options: Control responses to make selected flows deterministic
Replace all DOM events with synthetic clicks during browser runs
Guarantee real backend integrations are exercised
Increase screenshot resolution during failures
explanation: Mocking responses removes backend variability for stable tests.

prompt: Why is a test-id sometimes needed despite role/text queries?
options: A stable hook can identify otherwise ambiguous content
A test id is required for every interactive button on the page
Role queries cannot locate dynamically added elements
A test id makes inaccessible widgets accessible
explanation: When accessible queries are ambiguous, a dedicated test-id gives stability.

prompt: What is the tradeoff of E2E versus unit tests?
options: Broader integration coverage at higher execution cost
Faster execution with less coverage of application integrations
Identical coverage with a smaller setup cost
More isolation from browser and network behavior
explanation: E2E covers real flows but is heavier; balance with cheaper unit tests (the test pyramid).

prompt: Which command runs Playwright tests?
options: npx playwright test
npx playwright run
npm run e2e-playwright
playwright --start
explanation: The Playwright Test runner discovers and runs *.spec files.

prompt: Which command installs the browsers Playwright needs?
options: npx playwright install
npm install browsers
npx playwright setup-browsers
playwright download
explanation: Browsers are downloaded separately from the npm package.

prompt: What does page.click() do?
options: Clicks a selector match after actionability checks
Records a user click to generate and replay a browser test script
Clicks a fixed screen coordinate immediately
Dispatches a click on every matching element
explanation: Modern code usually calls locator.click() on a locator instead.

prompt: What does locator.fill() do?
options: Replaces a form control's current value with text
Appends keystrokes without clearing the field's existing value
Populates every text field in the current form
Sets the value without firing input events
explanation: fill focuses the field and sets its value in one step.

prompt: Which method takes a screenshot of the page?
options: page.screenshot()
page.capture()
page.image()
page.snapshot()
explanation: Screenshots help debug failures and power visual comparisons.

prompt: What does the headless mode mean?
options: The browser runs without a visible window
The browser runs without JavaScript enabled
The test runs without connecting to the network
The test runs without executing assertions
explanation: Headless is the default for speed; use --headed to watch.

prompt: What does the --headed flag do?
options: It shows the browser window during a test run
It shows only the final screenshot after tests
It starts the HTML reporter in a new window
It adds custom HTTP headers to requests
explanation: Headed mode is handy for watching a test locally.

prompt: Which file usually configures Playwright Test?
options: playwright.config.ts
playwright.json
.playwrightrc
package.json only
explanation: The config sets projects, base URL, retries, reporters and more.

prompt: What does expect(locator).toBeVisible() check?
options: The locator becomes visible before the timeout
The locator exists in source before page load
The locator matches an element in the viewport
The locator becomes enabled before the timeout
explanation: Web-first assertions retry automatically until they pass or time out.

prompt: What does expect(page).toHaveTitle() check?
options: The page's document title matches the expected value
The page's first heading matches the expected document title
The active test name matches the expected value
The browser project name matches the expected value
explanation: It accepts a string or regular expression.

prompt: What does expect(page).toHaveURL() verify?
options: The page's current URL matches the expected value
The configured baseURL matches the expected value
The last response URL matches the expected value
The hovered link target matches the expected value
explanation: Useful after navigation or redirects.

prompt: Which locator finds an element by its visible text?
options: page.getByText()
page.getByTag()
page.findText()
page.textSelector()
explanation: getByText matches visible text content.

prompt: Which locator finds a form field by its label?
options: page.getByLabel()
page.getByName()
page.getByField()
page.getByInput()
explanation: getByLabel mirrors how users find inputs.

prompt: What does test.describe() do in Playwright Test?
options: Groups related tests under a shared description
Prints each test's source code in the interactive HTML report
Creates a dedicated browser process per test
Documents the current page's DOM structure
explanation: Groups can share hooks and configuration.

prompt: What is codegen in Playwright?
options: A tool that records actions and generates test code
A tool that compiles TypeScript test files before browser execution
A tool that generates browser coverage summaries
A tool that checks code style in test files
explanation: npx playwright codegen opens a browser and writes code as you interact.

prompt: How does fill() differ from typing key by key (pressSequentially)?
options: fill replaces the value; pressSequentially sends keys
fill appends keys; pressSequentially replaces the value
Both APIs emit exactly the same keyboard events
pressSequentially sets the value without key events
explanation: Use key-by-key typing only when the app reacts to individual keystrokes.

prompt: What does the HTML reporter provide?
options: A browsable report with test results and attachments
A complete HTML validation report for every page in the suite
A generated site containing the tested application
A source coverage map rendered as an HTML page
explanation: Open it with npx playwright show-report.

prompt: What does locator.check() do?
options: Sets a checkbox or radio input to checked
Asserts that a matched element already exists
Checks the validity of the element's HTML
Submits a form and checks its server response
explanation: It asserts the element ends up checked.

prompt: What does locator.selectOption() do?
options: Chooses an option in a native select control
Chooses an element from a set of locators
Highlights text inside a contenteditable field
Opens a custom menu and clicks its first item
explanation: Options can be chosen by value, label or index.

prompt: What is baseURL used for in the config?
options: A base for resolving relative page navigation URLs
A proxy URL for all API calls made by the page under test
The path where Playwright stores its HTML report
The browser download location used during setup
explanation: It keeps tests environment-independent.

prompt: What are Playwright projects in the config?
options: Named test configurations for browsers or devices
Separate packages installed for each browser engine
Folders that hold fixtures for independent teams
Git branches created for parallel test workers
explanation: Projects let one suite run on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

prompt: How do you reuse a logged-in state across tests?
options: Capture storageState and use it in later test contexts
Reuse one page so its cookies survive across every test in the suite
Set a shared process variable with the login URL
Disable application authentication during test runs
explanation: A setup project can create the authenticated storage state.

prompt: What does page.route() let you do?
options: Intercept and handle matching network requests
Declare new routes in the application server
Navigate the browser between app screens
Rewrite the browser's DNS configuration
explanation: Routing makes tests independent of flaky backends.

prompt: What does locator.filter() do?
options: Narrow matches by text or descendant locators
Remove unwanted elements from the live DOM
Filter failed tests from the HTML report
Apply a visual filter to page screenshots
explanation: E.g. page.getByRole("listitem").filter({ hasText: "Milk" }).

prompt: What does test.beforeEach do in Playwright Test?
options: Run a setup hook before every test in its scope
Run a setup hook once before the test suite
Run a setup hook before every assertion
Run a setup hook once per browser process
explanation: Common for navigating to a starting page.

prompt: What does retries in the config do?
options: Rerun failing tests up to the configured count
Repeat every test even when its first run passes
Retry failed HTTP requests from the browser
Rerun a failed assertion without its test body
explanation: Retries reduce noise but can hide flakiness; tests that pass on retry are marked flaky.

prompt: What does trace: "on-first-retry" record?
options: Record a trace on the first retry of a failed test
Record a trace on every passing test's first run
Record only browser network logs on a retry
Record a trace only after all retries are exhausted
explanation: It captures debug data for failures without slowing every run.

prompt: What does expect(locator).toHaveText() do?
options: Retry an element text check until match or timeout
Type the expected text into the located element
Compare the page source against a text file
Read the element text without checking its value
explanation: It accepts strings, regexes or arrays for lists.

prompt: What does expect(locator).toHaveCount() check?
options: Check how many elements the locator currently matches
Check how many assertions the current test ran
Check how many browser requests were intercepted
Check how many worker processes are active
explanation: Useful for lists after filtering or deleting.

prompt: What is expect.soft() for?
options: Collect assertion failures and continue the test
Turn every failed assertion into a passing one
Retry the current assertion without a timeout
Skip later checks after the first failure
explanation: Soft assertions collect several failures in one run.

prompt: How do you wait for a specific network response?
options: Use page.waitForResponse() with a URL or predicate
Pause for a fixed delay and assume the response arrived
Wait until all browser network activity ends
Assert that a request was sent, without its response
explanation: Waiting on the actual response is more reliable than fixed timeouts.

prompt: Why avoid page.waitForTimeout in tests?
options: Fixed delays waste time and still miss slow conditions
Fixed delays turn every browser action into a retry
Fixed delays prevent DOM snapshots from being saved
Fixed delays are unsupported by Playwright Test
explanation: Prefer web-first assertions or waiting for events.

prompt: What does the webServer option in the config do?
options: Start an app server and await its ready endpoint
Host the HTML test report on the app's port
Proxy every test request through the dev server
Deploy the app to a remote environment first
explanation: Playwright can launch a dev server and reuse an existing one locally.

prompt: How do you emulate a mobile device?
options: Configure a project with a device descriptor
Resize the desktop browser window by hand
Install a mobile browser extension in each run
Use a real phone connected to the CI machine
explanation: Descriptors set viewport, user agent, touch and device scale factor.

prompt: What does page.getByPlaceholder() find?
options: Find inputs by their placeholder text
Find form fields by their label text
Find images by their alternative text
Find empty elements without any text
explanation: Prefer labels, but placeholders help when labels are missing.

prompt: What does locator.nth(i) do?
options: Choose one match by its zero-based position
Wait for the chosen match for i seconds
Retry the whole query exactly i times
Choose the i-th test in the current file
explanation: Use sparingly; order-based locators break when the UI changes.

prompt: What does test.use() do?
options: Set fixture options for a file or describe block
Import a package into every test in a file
Select browser binaries to download for CI
Enable a reporter plugin only for one test
explanation: It configures fixtures for the tests in its scope.

prompt: How can you upload a file in a Playwright test?
options: Set files on an input with locator.setInputFiles()
Send a file through a page.upload() browser method
Paste the local file path into the browser URL
Drag a file from the CI machine's desktop
explanation: setInputFiles also accepts in-memory buffers.

prompt: What does page.on("dialog") let you handle?
options: Handle JavaScript alert, confirm, and prompt dialogs
Handle every modal rendered by React components
Handle browser extension permission dialogs
Handle cookie banners built as page elements
explanation: By default dialogs are dismissed; a handler can accept them.

prompt: How do you run a single test file?
options: Pass the spec file path to the test command
Rename the file to include an only suffix
Use a --file-only option with no path
Comment out every other file in the suite
explanation: You can also filter by title with --grep.

prompt: Why do Playwright locators re-resolve on every action?
options: Resolve the locator again against the current DOM
Cache the first matching node for every later action
Reload the page before each interaction begins
Recreate the browser context after each click
explanation: Locators are lazy descriptions, not handles captured once.

prompt: What does strict mode for locators mean?
options: An action needs exactly one matched element
Every browser console warning fails the test
Only role based locators can be used in tests
Each page must finish loading within one second
explanation: Strictness prevents clicking the wrong element among several matches.

prompt: What does actionability checking verify before a click?
options: Visibility, stability, event target, and enabled state
A test id, an accessible name, and a click handler
A valid CSS rule and a position in the viewport
Successful network idle and an attached screenshot
explanation: These checks are why auto-waiting reduces flakiness.

prompt: How do worker-scoped fixtures differ from test-scoped fixtures?
options: One setup per worker shared by that worker's tests
One setup per browser page and every assertion
A separate fixture created for each test action
A fixture that runs only in the browser process
explanation: Use worker scope for expensive setup like a database per worker.

prompt: How would you handle tests that need unique data in parallel runs?
options: Give each test or worker its own data namespace
Share one account and serialize all tests globally
Clear the database after each individual assertion
Rely on whichever records the previous test made
explanation: Unique data avoids collisions between parallel workers.

prompt: What does fullyParallel: true change?
options: Permit tests in one file to run concurrently
Run each assertion in a separate worker process
Start every browser engine at the same instant
Launch each retry alongside the original test
explanation: Tests must then be fully independent of each other.

prompt: What is visual comparison with toHaveScreenshot()?
options: Compare a screenshot with a stored image baseline
Show screenshots next to each test in a report
Capture an image only when a test has failed
Record the browser viewport as a video file
explanation: Baselines are platform-specific; generate them in the same environment as CI.

prompt: Why are visual snapshots platform-sensitive?
options: Rendering and fonts can differ across environments
Playwright changes image pixels on every test run
Only Linux browsers support screenshot matching
Image files use different formats per browser
explanation: Run visual tests in a consistent container to avoid false diffs.

prompt: What does the request fixture (APIRequestContext) allow?
options: Make direct HTTP requests from the test process
Intercept browser requests without sending them
Configure DNS responses for browser contexts
Upload report screenshots to the CI server
explanation: API setup is faster and more reliable than doing it through the UI.

prompt: How can you test multiple users interacting at once?
options: Give each user a separate browser context and state
Open two tabs that share one authenticated session
Run one test file for each user in isolation
Use two browser engines for the same account
explanation: Contexts are isolated like separate incognito profiles.

prompt: What does page.clock (clock API) enable?
options: Control page time for timers and dates
Measure how long the test takes to execute
Change the timeout for one assertion
Synchronize the CI host's system clock
explanation: You can install a fake clock and fast-forward time in the browser.

prompt: How do you handle a new tab opened by a click?
options: Wait for a new page event as the click occurs
Read the original page after its URL changes
Restart the test in another browser project
Navigate back to the page that opened the tab
explanation: Promise.all or waitForEvent captures the popup page.

prompt: What is the risk of mocking every network call in E2E tests?
options: Mocks can hide faults in real frontend/backend integration
Mocked responses make every browser action slower
Mocks disable locator actionability and assertions
Browsers reject responses from intercepted requests
explanation: Mix: mock third parties and edge cases, but keep some true end-to-end paths.

prompt: What does test.step() add?
options: Add named steps visible in reports and traces
Run groups of subtests in parallel workers
Retry only actions inside the named step
Allocate a new context for each step
explanation: Steps make long flows easier to debug.

prompt: What does testInfo.attach() let you do?
options: Add logs or files to the test report
Attach a debugger to each browser worker
Register a new fixture for later tests
Link the test to a remote CI job
explanation: Attachments appear in the HTML report.

prompt: Why might hover-dependent UI be hard to test on mobile projects?
options: Hover only interfaces can be inaccessible on touch
Playwright cannot dispatch any hover interactions
Mobile browser projects cannot render CSS styles
Hover interactions require a visible browser window
explanation: This also reveals real accessibility issues for touch users.

prompt: How can you test accessibility with Playwright?
options: Use automated rules plus manual checks of key flows
Assume role locators prove the page is accessible
Compare screenshots as the only accessibility check
Expect Playwright to block inaccessible pages
explanation: Automated checks catch many issues but not all; manual review still matters.

prompt: What does globalSetup do?
options: Run a setup script once before the test suite
Run setup once before every individual test
Select the browser binary used for each test
Start the HTML report before every assertion
explanation: Setup projects are now often preferred because they appear in reports and traces.

prompt: Why should selectors avoid CSS classes generated by build tools?
options: Generated classes can change when styling is rebuilt
CSS classes cannot be selected by Playwright locators
WebKit executes CSS selectors much more slowly
Screenshots never show class based style changes
explanation: Role, label and text locators survive styling changes.

prompt: How do you debug a failing test interactively?
options: Use --debug or --ui to inspect test actions
Increase retries until one run finally passes
Print debug messages from the browser binary
Disable assertions while reproducing the issue
explanation: The inspector and UI mode show each action and the DOM at that moment.

prompt: How would you structure a large E2E suite to stay fast and trustworthy?
options: Keep critical journeys in E2E and isolate test data
Exercise every edge case through the browser UI
Share one login account among all parallel tests
Run the whole suite serially after every change
explanation: E2E is expensive; push detailed cases down to unit and integration tests.

prompt: How do you make E2E tests independent of test order and each other?
options: Create isolated data without test order dependencies
Run the suite in alphabetical filename order
Reset shared staging state only once per day
Force every describe block into serial mode
explanation: Independence enables parallelism, sharding and targeted reruns.

prompt: How should authentication be handled in a big suite with several roles?
options: Prepare storage states for each role in setup
Use the same admin credentials for every role
Complete the full login UI flow before each step
Disable authorization checks in the test server
explanation: Role-specific states keep tests fast while exercising permissions.

prompt: How do you decide what belongs in E2E versus component tests?
options: Use E2E for integrated journeys and components for UI states
Put every validation edge case in a browser flow
Use only component tests for cross-service journeys
Choose test type by whichever runner is already open
explanation: The test pyramid balances confidence with speed and cost.

prompt: What are good practices for testing against a shared staging environment?
options: Namespace and clean test data in shared staging
Delete all staging records before each CI run
Assume another team's records never change
Schedule tests only when the office is closed
explanation: Shared environments drift; tests must tolerate or control their data.

prompt: How do you use traces to diagnose CI-only failures?
options: Capture traces on retry and inspect steps and network
Increase all timeouts until the CI test passes
Turn off parallelism without examining the failure
Repeat local runs and discard the CI trace
explanation: Traces capture the exact CI conditions without reproducing locally.

prompt: When is it appropriate to use a test id attribute despite accessibility-first locators?
options: Use a test id when no stable user-facing query fits
Use test ids for every element because they run faster
Avoid test ids even when the accessible name changes
Use a test id only for disabled button elements
explanation: Test ids are a pragmatic fallback, but missing accessible names may also be a bug.

prompt: How do you test a feature behind a feature flag in E2E?
options: Set the flag per test and cover critical states
Wait until the flag is removed from the product
Test only the enabled variant on developer laptops
Toggle production flags manually before each CI job
explanation: Deterministic flag control keeps tests reproducible.

prompt: How would you catch visual regressions without drowning in false positives?
options: Use focused baselines, masks, and stable rendering
Capture every whole page at each action and compare
Allow large pixel drift so every snapshot passes
Compare images from arbitrary developer machines
explanation: Masking timestamps and ads prevents noise; consistent rendering prevents drift.

prompt: How do you balance retries with flakiness detection?
options: Track tests that pass only after a small retry
Increase retries until CI looks consistently green
Disable retries and ignore recurring transient fails
Retry only when a developer runs the suite locally
explanation: Retries protect the pipeline; tracking prevents normalizing flakiness.

prompt: How can E2E tests verify emails or SMS sent by the app?
options: Read messages from a test inbox or capture API
Ask a tester to check a real phone manually
Assume successful form submit implies delivery
Intercept the browser's nonexistent SMS inbox
explanation: Test inboxes let tests read codes or links programmatically.

prompt: What are the risks of running E2E tests against production?
options: Real data and side effects may be changed by tests
Production browsers refuse automation by default
A green production test proves no user was affected
Production runs cannot generate noisy metrics
explanation: Synthetic monitoring in prod needs dedicated accounts and safe, read-mostly flows.

prompt: How do you test cross-browser differences efficiently?
options: Run critical journeys across supported engines
Run every edge case on every device permutation
Check only the engine used by the CI server
Defer differences until users report broken flows
explanation: Target the engines your users use and where behavior genuinely differs.

prompt: How would you design page objects without over-abstracting?
options: Share stable interactions while keeping tests readable
Wrap every locator and assertion behind a method
Put every page's behavior in one base class
Duplicate all interactions in each individual test
explanation: Thin page objects reduce duplication without hiding what tests check.

prompt: How do you keep E2E test data realistic yet deterministic?
options: Use realistic fixtures with deterministic identities
Copy live production data into the suite nightly
Generate entirely random records on every run
Depend on fixed record IDs in shared staging
explanation: Realistic, reproducible data catches bugs without flakiness.

prompt: What is the value of running a smoke subset on every deploy?
options: Check core deployed journeys with a small suite
Replace all integration and unit tests with smoke
Measure throughput of every deployed endpoint
Guarantee every feature and edge case is working
explanation: A small, stable smoke suite gives quick signal after each deployment.

prompt: How do you test offline or slow-network behavior?
options: Simulate offline mode and controlled response delays
Disconnect the CI machine from its network entirely
Assume mobile browser profiles are always offline
Delay every test with a global fixed timeout
explanation: Simulating network conditions reveals missing loading and error states.

prompt: How should secrets be handled in E2E pipelines?
options: Load test account secrets from a CI secret store
Commit test account secrets beside the spec files
Print the credentials into every failure report
Reuse developer accounts in every CI environment
explanation: Use dedicated test accounts and CI secret storage; traces and reports may need masking.

prompt: How do you prevent E2E tests from coupling to copy text that marketing changes?
options: Use stable interaction hooks and assert copy where it matters
Freeze all marketing copy so tests stay green
Use numeric XPath indexes instead of labels
Avoid asserting any user-facing text at all
explanation: Use roles and stable names where possible; if names change often, a test id can keep interaction tests independent of copy.

prompt: What signals that an E2E suite needs restructuring?
options: Growing runtime, flaky reruns, and overlapping coverage
A stable runtime and few failures across CI runs
A small smoke suite with clear ownership
Independent tests with isolated setup data
explanation: Health metrics guide pruning and moving tests down the pyramid.

prompt: What is Jest?
options: A framework for running and asserting JavaScript tests
A framework for bundling and optimizing JavaScript for browsers
A framework for linting JavaScript source files
A framework for automating full browser journeys
explanation: Jest runs JS/TS tests with assertions, mocks, and coverage.

prompt: Which function defines a single test?
options: test() or its it() alias
describe() or its suite() alias
expect() with a matcher
beforeEach() with a hook
explanation: test (alias it) declares an individual test case.

prompt: What groups related tests?
options: describe() groups related tests
expect() groups related matchers
beforeEach() groups setup hooks
jest.fn() groups mock calls
explanation: describe blocks organize related tests.

prompt: What makes an assertion?
options: Calling a matcher on expect(value)
describe() registers a new test without checking an outcome
jest.fn() creates a test result
beforeAll() verifies setup state
explanation: expect(value).matcher() asserts expectations.

prompt: What runs setup before each test?
options: beforeEach() runs before each test
beforeAll() runs once before all tests in its scope
afterEach() runs after each test in its scope
describe() groups tests without running a setup hook
explanation: beforeEach runs prior to every test in scope.

prompt: What is a mock?
options: A stand-in with controlled behavior and call tracking
A real dependency called during integration tests
A stored rendering used by snapshot assertions
A report of source lines run during tests
explanation: Mocks replace dependencies to isolate the unit under test.

prompt: What does jest.fn() create?
options: A mock function with configurable behavior
A new test suite with inherited hooks
A controllable clock for asynchronous code
A stored snapshot for rendered output
explanation: jest.fn() makes a tracked mock function.

prompt: What is a snapshot test?
options: A comparison against output saved previously
A measurement of elapsed runtime for every test assertion
A replacement for an external HTTP service
A check that source types compile correctly
explanation: Snapshots record serialized output and flag changes on later runs.

prompt: How do toBe and toEqual differ?

prompt: What is the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern?
options: Set up, perform the behavior, then verify its result
Verify the result before setting up any test state or action
Deploy the app, run it, then inspect its logs
Review source code, approve it, then merge it
explanation: AAA keeps tests easy to read and consistent.

prompt: What does "fake it till you make it" mean in TDD?
options: Start with a simple constant, then generalize through tests
Pretend tests pass without actually running the suite
Mock every collaborator before writing behavior
Skip the refactor step after the first green run
explanation: It's a legitimate small step toward the real implementation.

prompt: What is triangulation in TDD?
options: Add examples that force a more general implementation
Run the same browser test on three different rendering engines
Write exactly three assertions for each function
Measure source coverage with three separate tools
explanation: A second or third case exposes hard-coded shortcuts.

prompt: Why keep tests fast in TDD?
options: Frequent runs need a short, reliable feedback loop
Faster tests use less disk space in the repository
CI systems refuse to execute slow test suites
Slow tests cannot fail for a meaningful reason
explanation: TDD relies on feedback in seconds.

prompt: What should happen when a new test passes immediately without code changes?
options: Check whether the behavior exists or the test is weak
Assume the implementation is complete and stop
Delete the passing test without reviewing it
Add unrelated assertions until something fails
explanation: A test never seen failing might not test what you think.

prompt: What is a test list in TDD?
options: A list of behaviors to test next as work evolves
A list of CI jobs needed before deployment
A record of flaky tests from the last run
The generated coverage report for a release
explanation: Kent Beck keeps a list to stay focused on one test at a time.

prompt: What is a unit in TDD often considered to be?
options: A cohesive behavior that may span several classes
Exactly one method regardless of its callers
Exactly one source file regardless of behavior
One line of executable production code
explanation: Focusing on behavior avoids tests tied to structure.

prompt: Why is TDD considered a design practice as well as a testing practice?
options: The first caller test shapes an API's usability
Writing tests automatically produces UML diagrams
Writing tests removes all architecture decisions
Testing only checks results after design is done
explanation: Hard-to-test code is often a design signal.

prompt: What is a failing test's error message useful for?
options: It confirms the failure is for the intended reason
It measures the runtime of the failing test
It generates user facing documentation
It chooses implementation variable names
explanation: A test failing for the wrong reason can mislead you.

prompt: What does "baby steps" mean in TDD?
options: Change one small thing, then rerun the tests
Write tests only as a junior engineer
Type the assertions at a slower speed
Restrict every project to tiny features
explanation: Small steps make it obvious which change broke something.

prompt: Which kind of test is most common in TDD cycles?
options: Fast tests around a small behavior boundary
Manual exploratory sessions for each feature
Load tests for every method implementation
Full browser journeys on every edit
explanation: Fast tests keep the red-green-refactor loop tight.

prompt: What does a green bar mean?
options: The current suite passes its checks
The code has optimal runtime behavior
The feature is deployed to production
The code has exactly full coverage
explanation: Green is the safe state to refactor from.

prompt: Should production code be written without a failing test in strict TDD?
options: In strict TDD, add behavior through a failing test
In strict TDD, write tests only after the code
In strict TDD, UI changes never need tests
In strict TDD, test order depends on the day
explanation: In strict TDD each behavior change is driven by a test.

prompt: What is a "test double"?
options: An object that stands in for a dependency
A test duplicated in two separate files
The same test executed two times
A test that contains two assertions
explanation: Stubs, mocks, fakes and spies are kinds of test doubles.

prompt: What is a fake in testing?
options: A working simplified stand-in, such as in-memory storage
A test written only to pass without assertions
Production data fabricated for staging tests
A test disabled until a later release
explanation: Fakes behave realistically but take shortcuts unsuitable for production.

prompt: What is the benefit of naming tests after behaviors?
options: Names document the behavior a test protects
Names cause each test to execute more quickly in the test runner
Names make every test sort alphabetically
Names are required by every test framework
explanation: Good names turn the suite into living documentation.

prompt: What is the "transformation priority premise"?
options: Apply simple code transformations before complex ones
Refactor the whole design before running tests
Convert the tests into production source code
Choose runtime optimized algorithms first
explanation: Uncle Bob's premise helps keep TDD steps small and well-ordered.

prompt: What is outside-in TDD?
options: Start from an outer acceptance need to drive inner units
Start with database details and later test the UI
Write unit tests before deciding any user behavior
Test only external APIs without inner code
explanation: An outer acceptance test can guide smaller tests; mockist TDD is one outside-in style.

prompt: What characterizes the "classicist" (Detroit) school of TDD?
options: Use real collaborators and verify resulting state
Mock every dependency and verify call sequences
Write all tests only after production code exists
Test only through a rendered browser interface
explanation: Classicists mock mainly at awkward boundaries like I/O.

prompt: What is the double-loop TDD approach?
options: An outer acceptance loop around inner unit cycles
Run every test twice before each code change
Have two developers write the same test
Run the same suite in two CI environments
explanation: The acceptance test defines "done" while unit tests drive design.

prompt: Why write one assertion concept per test?
options: One behavior per test helps localize a failure
Frameworks permit exactly one assertion call within each test
Several assertions always slow a test down
A test should check only one private method
explanation: Several asserts are fine if they check the same concept.

prompt: What is the role of refactoring the tests themselves?
options: Keep tests clear and remove avoidable duplication
Avoid refactoring test code after it has first passed in CI
Delete assertions to make the test run faster
Convert test setup into production behavior
explanation: Test code quality matters because tests are read and changed often.

prompt: How does TDD handle a bug report?
options: Reproduce the bug in a failing test, then fix it
Fix the code and leave the report untested
Add tests only for future unrelated features
Revert the product to its last release
explanation: The test proves the fix and prevents regression.

prompt: What is an "obvious implementation" in TDD?
options: Write the clear implementation once a test demands it
Copy any apparently working implementation found on the internet
Implement the feature before adding a test
Use the first design even if the test is awkward
explanation: Beck allows larger steps when confident, shrinking them when surprised.

prompt: What is a "learning test"?
options: A test used to understand a third party API
A test written only for a student exercise
A test that trains a machine learning model
A test allowed to run exactly one time
explanation: Learning tests also detect changes when you upgrade the library.

prompt: Why avoid testing private methods directly in TDD?
options: Check public behavior instead of private structure
Private methods can never contain defects
Testing a private method always needs a browser
Frameworks prohibit any private method access
explanation: If a private method needs direct tests, it may belong in its own unit.

prompt: What is a "walking skeleton"?
options: A thin end to end slice that proves integration
A test with no assertion and no expected result
A framework generated class with empty methods
A prototype deliberately discarded after a demo
explanation: Starting with a skeleton gives acceptance tests something real to drive.

prompt: How does TDD relate to continuous integration?
options: Small tested changes support frequent integration
TDD replaces the need for any CI pipeline
CI prevents developers from writing tests first
The practices cannot be used together
explanation: A fast, trusted suite is what makes frequent merging safe.

prompt: What is "test-first" versus "test-driven"?
options: Test first sets order; test driven also shapes design
The phrases always mean exactly the same development practice
Test first means writing only unit level tests
Test driven means no refactor step is allowed
explanation: TDD includes the refactor step, not just ordering.

prompt: Why is the refactor step often skipped, and why does it matter?
options: Stopping at green can let design debt accumulate
The refactor step is prohibited by strict TDD
Refactoring necessarily makes the suite fail
Code tools always refactor automatically
explanation: Without refactoring TDD produces tested but messy code.

prompt: What does "red-green-refactor" say about when to add new behavior?
options: Introduce behavior through a new failing test
Introduce behavior while restructuring green code
Introduce behavior only after deployment
Introduce behavior without checking the suite
explanation: Refactoring changes structure only; behavior changes start with red.

prompt: How can TDD help define an API before it exists?
options: Calling an API as a client reveals awkward signatures
Writing tests generates complete API documentation by itself
Tests eliminate any need to design an interface
TDD can only test APIs that already exist
explanation: Using the API first shows how pleasant it is to call.

prompt: What is a "humble object" pattern used for in TDD?
options: Move logic out of hard to test UI or I/O shells
Limit every class to fewer than ten lines
Avoid all inheritance in domain code
Give objects deliberately modest names
explanation: The remaining humble shell is thin and barely needs testing.

prompt: What is mutation testing used for in a TDD context?
options: Check whether tests catch small code mutations
Run tests of evolutionary algorithms only
Randomly change the order of test files
Mutate fixture data without assertions
explanation: Surviving mutants reveal weak or missing assertions.

prompt: How does TDD handle external services like email?
options: Use a test double locally and verify integration separately
Call the real email provider from every unit test
Skip any code that sends external messages
Replace the host network card during tests
explanation: Isolation keeps TDD fast while integration tests verify the real service.

prompt: What is "test coverage" in TDD practice typically a result of?
options: Coverage follows tests that exercise behavior
Coverage percentage is the sole goal of TDD
Coverage must always be maximized at any cost
Coverage is irrelevant to test feedback
explanation: TDD tends to yield high coverage without targeting it directly.

prompt: Why can London-school TDD lead to brittle tests?
options: Interaction heavy mocks can couple tests to call structure
Classicist tests cannot use any test doubles
London school tests only database behavior
Interaction checks require snapshot baselines
explanation: Mocks verify how objects talk, so restructuring breaks many tests.

prompt: How do you apply TDD to a bug in a legacy system with no tests?
options: Characterize the area, reproduce the bug, then fix
Rewrite the whole legacy system before adding tests
Patch first and add tests after the next release
Use only an E2E test for every legacy behavior
explanation: Pin existing behavior before changing it.

prompt: What is the "test pyramid" and how does TDD relate to it?
options: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration and E2E tests
Equal numbers of unit, integration, and E2E tests
A suite composed mostly of full browser tests
A filename order for running all test levels
explanation: TDD's fast feedback comes from the wide base.

prompt: Why is TDD harder for UI layout and visual design?
options: Visual quality can resist precise automated assertions
React interfaces cannot be tested at any level
UI frameworks ban tests for layout decisions
Layout is fixed and therefore needs no tests
explanation: Test behavior and logic via TDD; use visual and manual review for appearance.

prompt: What does "listen to the tests" mean?
options: Use test writing pain as feedback about design
Read each passing test result out loud
Ask users to vote on test implementation
Play a sound whenever a test turns green
explanation: From "Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests".

prompt: How do you avoid over-specifying tests in TDD?
options: Assert important outcomes, not incidental internals
Assert every field of every returned object
Replace behavior checks with large snapshots
Mock all collaborators to fix call structure
explanation: Over-specified tests fail for irrelevant changes.

prompt: What's the difference between TDD and ATDD?
options: ATDD uses shared acceptance examples; TDD drives code
ATDD and TDD are exactly the same practice
ATDD omits tests and uses only requirements
TDD can be applied only to user interface code
explanation: ATDD focuses on shared understanding of requirements.

prompt: How can TDD be applied to database code?
options: Test repository behavior with a suitable test database
Mock SQL statement strings without executing them
Skip tests for data access and persistence
Run database tests only against production
explanation: Integration tests verify queries; domain logic stays fast to test.

prompt: Why might strict TDD slow down exploratory prototyping?
options: Changing discoveries can force many test rewrites
TDD prevents all exploratory prototypes
Prototypes cannot compile alongside tests
A spike is forbidden by any TDD process
explanation: Many teams spike to learn, then throw the spike away and TDD the real code.

prompt: What is a "spike" in agile development?
options: A time limited learning experiment
A sudden rise in production bug reports
A test measuring peak system performance
A long running branch for an entire feature
explanation: After a spike, TDD rebuilds the solution with tests.

prompt: How does TDD encourage dependency injection?
options: Passing collaborators in makes substitutions easy
TDD requires a dedicated dependency injection framework to run
Dependency injection replaces the need for tests
TDD forbids using object constructors
explanation: Testability pressure pushes toward explicit dependencies.

prompt: What is the risk of mocking value objects?
options: Mocking them adds coupling where real values suffice
Value objects cannot be replaced by doubles in any language
Mocking values always improves test clarity
Mocks greatly speed up primitive comparisons
explanation: Mock roles and boundaries, not simple data.

prompt: What does "test behavior, not methods" imply for test structure?
options: Organize tests around scenarios and outcomes
Write exactly one test for every method
Test only public methods without scenarios
Mirror every source class in the test tree
explanation: Behavior-oriented tests survive method renames and splits.

prompt: How should a TDD practitioner handle a test that is hard to write?
options: Treat difficulty as possible coupling or unclear boundaries
Skip any test that looks difficult to write
Write all production code before checking behavior
Mock every object to force the test to pass
explanation: Hard-to-test code often has too many responsibilities.

prompt: Why is property-based testing a useful complement to example-based TDD?
options: Generated examples check invariants and edge cases
Property checks replace all concrete examples
Property testing is only for benchmark suites
Generated tests need no expected conditions
explanation: E.g. sorting output is ordered and a permutation of the input.

prompt: What is "defect localization" and why does TDD help it?
options: Small tests and steps narrow where a defect began
Translate failure text into the local language
Assign each defect to a team by file location
Store all bugs alongside their source line
explanation: When the last small change breaks a test, the cause is obvious.

prompt: How does TDD interact with continuous refactoring in legacy code?
options: Add tests near each change to grow safe coverage
Test the entire legacy system before any edit
Avoid using TDD on all legacy code
Stop refactoring once characterization starts
explanation: Coverage grows where the code actually changes.

prompt: Why keep test setup minimal and explicit?
options: Visible setup shows which conditions matter
Testing frameworks limit setup to one statement
Shared setup cannot be used in any test suite
Minimal setup guarantees parallel execution
explanation: Hidden or bloated setup hides the essence of a test.

prompt: What does "the test is the first client" mean?
options: Tests call an interface before production callers do
Only external clients are allowed to write tests
Users run every test before using a feature
The first test is billed to the product client
explanation: Designing for the first client tends to give usable APIs.

prompt: How can a team measure whether TDD is paying off?
options: Track defects, lead time, and refactoring confidence
Count tests as the sole measure of improvement
Measure test source lines but ignore defects
Compare coverage values across unrelated teams
explanation: Outcomes like fewer regressions matter more than activity metrics.

prompt: How do you introduce TDD into a team that doesn't practice it?
options: Start small, pair on real work, and compare outcomes
Require full coverage before anyone can merge a feature branch
Rewrite all legacy modules before trying TDD
Mandate the practice without providing support
explanation: Skills and visible benefits drive adoption more than rules.

prompt: How do you decide the right granularity of tests when practicing TDD?
options: Test cohesive behavior at a stable boundary
Write exactly one test for each source class
Write exactly one test for every public method
Use only full system acceptance tests
explanation: The unit should be a behavior with a stable contract.

prompt: How can TDD coexist with a strong type system?
options: Types catch structural errors; tests check behavior
Static types make automated tests unnecessary
Tests make compile time type checks unnecessary
A strong type system cannot be used with TDD
explanation: Types and tests are complementary forms of specification.

prompt: What's the risk of treating coverage targets as the goal of TDD?
options: Targets can reward shallow tests that only run lines
Targets necessarily lower the coverage percentage
Targets prevent a suite from running quickly
Targets make every refactor impossible
explanation: Coverage is a byproduct; asserting behavior is the goal.

prompt: How do you use TDD for concurrent or asynchronous code?
options: Control scheduling and time; add stress checks separately
Use fixed sleeps to order concurrent operations
Avoid checking concurrent behavior in any test
Rerun flaky cases until one result looks correct
explanation: Deterministic control makes race conditions reproducible.

prompt: How does TDD influence architecture over the long term?
options: Tests often encourage clear boundaries and interfaces
TDD dictates that every system use microservices
TDD cannot influence architecture at any level
TDD requires a particular layered monolith
explanation: Testability pressure favors modularity and explicit dependencies.

prompt: When is it reasonable not to TDD a piece of code?
options: When a test costs more than its value for throwaway code
Never, every line must start from a failing test
Whenever a deadline approaches for any feature
For every component in a user interface
explanation: Pragmatism: choose where TDD yields the most value.

prompt: How do you keep a large TDD suite from slowing development?
options: Keep local tests fast and stage slower checks
Run the complete CI suite after every single keystroke
Delete all integration checks to save time
Add CI machines without profiling slow tests
explanation: Fast inner-loop tests plus staged slower tests preserve flow.

prompt: How do you avoid mocks that lie about real dependency behavior?
options: Run shared contracts against the double and real service
Update the mock only after a production failure
Ban all fakes and stubs in every test
Assume generated mocks always match production
explanation: Contract tests keep mocks honest as dependencies evolve.

prompt: How does TDD help with emergent design versus big upfront design?
options: Evolve design in small tested steps as evidence grows
Stop considering design once tests are written
Complete all architecture before the first test
Expect every TDD team to reach identical design
explanation: Emergent design still needs deliberate refactoring and judgment.

prompt: How do you handle tests that break because requirements changed?
options: Update tests to specify the newly required behavior
Delete failing tests without reviewing intent
Keep old tests red as permanent reminders
Revert the requirement to make the suite green
explanation: Tests encode requirements; changing requirements means changing tests.

prompt: Why might pairing or mob programming amplify TDD's benefits?
options: Continuous feedback keeps steps and tests focused
Pairing doubles test execution speed in CI
Mob work removes the refactor step from TDD
Collaboration reduces the need for any tests
explanation: Shared attention prevents skipping steps like refactoring.

prompt: How do you TDD code involving randomness or current time?
options: Inject a clock or random source the test can control
Use actual wall time and accept intermittent fails
Avoid writing tests for any randomized behavior
Schedule test runs at the same hour every day
explanation: Injection turns nondeterminism into ordinary inputs.

prompt: How do you balance speed of delivery with TDD discipline under deadlines?
options: Protect critical behavior and reduce scope if needed
Stop writing tests until after the deadline
Double the team size to offset every test
Check only after a production release
explanation: Skipping tests usually shifts cost to later debugging.

prompt: What's the value of the "fourth step" some add to TDD: thinking before red?
options: Select the next test to guide design deliberately
Write the full user documentation before coding
Prepare a deployment plan before the red phase
Measure source coverage before any test exists
explanation: Picking the right next test is a key skill in TDD.

prompt: How can TDD support safe large-scale refactoring?
options: A trustworthy suite supports checked, incremental changes
A test suite makes all refactoring unnecessary
TDD forbids reorganizing large modules
Tests automatically restructure source code
explanation: Confidence to change is TDD's main long-term payoff.

prompt: How do you test-drive error handling and edge cases without bloating the suite?
options: Group related edge cases in parameterized tests
Write a separate test for every possible input value and state
Leave all edge cases for manual exploration
Test only successful paths while writing code
explanation: Table-driven tests keep many cases concise.

prompt: How do BDD-style specifications and TDD reinforce each other?
options: Shared BDD examples guide focused implementation tests
BDD replaces all TDD tests once specs exist
BDD and TDD cannot be practiced together
TDD automatically writes all BDD scenarios
explanation: Outer behavior specs plus inner TDD create the double loop.

prompt: Why does TDD benefit from a fast, reliable build pipeline?
options: Small changes need rapid feedback in local and CI runs
TDD works without any pipeline feedback
Pipelines replace tests run by developers
Slow feedback makes the process more disciplined
explanation: Fast CI keeps integration continuous and problems small.

prompt: How do you judge whether a test adds value or should be deleted?
options: Keep tests that protect important behavior affordably
Preserve every test forever, including obsolete ones
Delete all tests once they are a year old
Keep only tests that have failed in CI before
explanation: Low-value, brittle tests cost more than they protect.
